lesson.title: Networks of Networks: What Makes an Autonomous System
lesson.summary: An autonomous system is a network operated under single administrative control with its own routing policy, identified by an AS number, and it is the basic unit that BGP connects across the internet.
lesson.body:
Every BGP advertisement carries an AS path, a list of autonomous system numbers, but it is worth pausing on what an autonomous system actually is, because it is the fundamental organizational unit that all of interdomain routing is built around. An autonomous system, or AS, is a network or group of networks operated under a single technical administration, with its own internally consistent routing policy, that presents a single, coherent block of address space to the rest of the internet. A university, a large corporation, a cloud provider, and an internet service provider might each be an autonomous system, or a large ISP might comprise several. What matters is not size, but administrative unity: within an AS, someone can freely choose whatever interior routing protocol suits them, commonly OSPF, and that choice is invisible to and irrelevant to everyone else.

The reason the internet is organized this way, rather than as one flat network, follows directly from why path vector routing and BGP exist in the first place. No single router, and no single organization, can hold a real time, trustworthy map of the entire internet the way an OSPF router holds a map of its own domain. The internet is far too large, changes far too continuously, and spans far too many independent, non-cooperating administrative entities for that kind of flooding and trust to work. Carving the internet into autonomous systems solves this by hiding complexity: everything happening inside an AS, however large or however it is routed internally, is summarized to the outside world as one participant with one AS number, reachable via the routes its border routers choose to advertise. Other autonomous systems do not need to know or care whether an AS runs OSPF or something else internally, or how many routers it has, they only need to know that the AS exists as an addressable, policy bearing unit in the AS path.

Each AS is identified by an autonomous system number, assigned by a regional internet registry, which BGP uses to identify it uniquely in every AS path advertisement. Originally these numbers were 16 bits wide, allowing a bit over sixty five thousand values, and the number space has since been extended to 32 bits as the internet grew past that original supply. The AS number is what makes loop detection in path vector routing work: a router can check whether its own AS number already appears in an advertised path. It is also what makes policy possible, since an operator's routing policy is naturally expressed in terms of which neighboring autonomous systems to prefer, trust, or avoid, not in terms of individual routers or links the way interior routing policy is.
